thread.title: Dow Drops 2%, but U.S. Is Winning the Trade War

author: Ben Levisohn
title: Dow Drops 2%, but U.S. Is Winning the Trade War
text:
Photo: Getty Images By Ben Levisohn June 23, 2018 Vital Signs
Is this what winning looks like?
Sure, the Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 509.59 points, or 2%, to 24,580.89 last week as concerns about an escalation in trade tensions helped sink the market. The S&P 500 fell 0.9%, to 2754.88, and the Nasdaq Composite declined 0.7%, to 7692.82, to end a four-week winning streak.
But consider how much worse it could have been. China’s Shanghai Composite Index, for one, fell 4.4%, to 2889.76 last week, and is now down 13% in 2018. The S&P 500, by contrast, is up 3.3% this year.
Better still, the U.S., because of its more-developed markets, has more corners where investors can hide from the worst of the trade spat. The Russell 2000, for instance, has gained 9.8% this year as investors shift away from internationally exposed large-caps to small companies that do most of their business in the U.S.
“The market has to wait this out,” says Quincy Krosby, chief market strategist at Prudential Financial. “And small-caps have been the trade-war safety trade.”
The U.S. market’s resilience suggests that investors suspect the U.S. has the upper hand. So far, the tariffs that have been announced have been tit-for-tat, with the U.S. announcing tariffs on $50 billion worth of Chinese goods, and China responding with tariffs on $50 billion of U.S. products. The Trump administration is also considering imposing penalties on an additional $200 billion of Chinese products. China can respond to that with more tariffs, but would find itself rapidly running out of goods to tax, given that it imported only $130 billion from the U.S. in 2017.
China has other measures it could use, but many of them could prove to be self-defeating. It could, if it wanted, offset the tariffs by causing its currency to drop by 6% to 10%, Gavekal’s Tom Holland wrote in a report last week, but that would probably cause investors to abandon China’s financial markets. It could try to dump its U.S. Treasury holdings, but if it sold them in bits and pieces, the market could easily absorb them, and if it tried to sell them all at once, it might find no buyers at all. And urging Chinese consumers to boycott U.S. products—something that the government did in 2012 with Japanese goods—would hurt Chinese workers, since Apple (ticker: AAPL), Procter & Gamble (PG), and Caterpillar (CAT) manufacture most of their goods for China’s markets locally, while McDonald’s (MCD) owns just 20% of its Chinese business.
“That won’t stop Beijing pursuing retaliation,” Holland explained. “But the effectiveness of such retaliation will be limited, and the costs high.”
Newsletter Sign-up China does have one advantage. Because President Xi Jinping doesn’t need to worry about elections, he doesn’t have to worry about getting thrown out of office if tariffs cause consumers pain, explains Bank of America Merrill Lynch economist Aditya Bhave. Trump has to worry about getting re-elected in 2020, while members of the U.S. House of Representatives face elections every two years.
That’s another way of saying this trade war is a long way from being over.
